newsitem.title: FINLAND: World steelmakers upbeat on can market prospects.
newsitem.headline: World steelmakers upbeat on can market prospects.

text.p: Steel executives on Wednesday were optimistic about prospects for clawing back a share of the beverage can market from aluminium, and outlined strategies for battle at a conference here.

Top executives from the world's steelmakers at the annual conference of the International Iron and Steel Institute heard that tinplate producers had convinced customers in Britain, Italy and Israel to convert six lines to steel in two years.

This is the equivalent of three billion cans or 100,000 tonnes per year, Jost Massenberg, board member from Germany's Rasselstein Hoesch GmbH said in a statement summarising his speech made available to reporters before the conference.
"Customers are envisaging the conversion of an additional 10 lines, representing a further 150,000 tonnes of tinplate per year," he said in the statement.

The beverage can market will remain dynamic with four percent growth annually, he said. Although competition would remain keen -- intensifying also from plastics -- he said customers looking to diversify were an opportunity.

Christophe Cornier, director of planning and strategy and packaging steels at Sollac, France, said the steel can had overtaken its rival in Europe with a 55 percent share of the market, up from 45 percent a year ago.

Aluminium industry executives at a similar event last May heard the opposite -- Bernard Legrand of the European Aluminium Association said in Duesseldorf that aluminium had 55 percent of the European market, up from 37 percent in 1985.
But speakers at the steel conference agreed that aluminium still totally dominates the U.S. market.
Cornier said the diversity of packaging materials -- metals, glass, and the plastic PET -- outside the United States "implies that the competition remains open, especially within Europe".
"The superior mechanical performance of the steel can over aluminium and PET is its main advantage," he said in the summary of his speech.

European can producers have managed to thin down can walls to reduce the average can body weight to 25 grammes in 1996 from 29 grammes in 1990, he said: a 30 percent reduction in body weight generally means a 10 percent cut in total can cost.

"At present, the potential for lightweighting cans is 30 percent for steel," he said. "It is five percent for aluminium, with no modifications of filler equipment and processes, or 10 percent otherwise."
"The reduction in cost due to wall thinning is equivalent to $4 for steel (10 percent of the cost of packaging) and $2 for aluminium (five percent of the cost of packaging)," he said.
Both steel and aluminium costs could also come down by $2 more if rolling productivity is optimised, he said.

Takashi Asamura, managing director of Nippon Steel Corp's technical development bureau, said film-laminated cans offered an ideal way to reduce manufacturing costs for steel; which he said has 60 percent of the Japanese beverage market.
Describing a Japanese film-laminated can known as the "Tokyo Ultimate Can" (TULC), he said the investment was cheaper than in aluminium.

"The initial investment cost of a TULC canmaking line is 80 percent of that of the aluminium line, the number of operators and energy can be reduced by 40 percent and 60 percent respectively, and the overall process cost is about 30 percent less," he said in the summary of his speech.

"Laminate cans are lightly tin-coated steel cans with a beautiful, pressure-bonded photogravure film which gives the can a high commercial value," he said. One company he mentioned, called Daiwa Can, could supply strip for 17 can welding lines and plans to build a second line, he said.
